Guidance is a specific financial or operating forecast, target or outlook stated or clearly confirmed by company management. Include numerical and meaningful qualitative forecasts, reaffirmations, withdrawals, and qualifications that change a forecast's meaning. Exclude actual results, merely recalled old forecasts, analyst-only estimates, vague optimism and boilerplate. A hypothetical illustration is not a committed forecast. Resolve references using the entire call; do not invent missing facts.

[P000] [S0000] Operator [0]: Good morning and welcome to Ali's Bargain Outlet Conference call to discuss financial results for the fourth quarter and fiscal year 2024. [S0001] Currently, all participants are in listen-only mode. [S0002] Later, we will conduct a question and answer session and interactive instructions will be provided at that time. [S0003] Please be advised that this call is being recorded and the reproduction of this call in whole or in part is not permitted without the express written authorization of Ali's. [S0004] Joining us on today's call from OLLI's management are Eric Vandervalk, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Robert Helm, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. [S0005] Certain comments made today may constitute forward-looking statements and are made pursuant to and within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 as amended. [S0006] Such forward-looking statements are subject to both known and unknown risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from such statements. [S0007] These risks and uncertainties are described in our annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q on file with the SEC and earnings press releases. [S0008] Forward-looking statements are made today as of the date of this call, and we do not undertake any obligation to update these statements. [S0009] On today's call, the company will also refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures. [S0010] Reconciliation of the most closely comparable GAAP financial measures to non-GAAP financial measures are included in our earnings press release. [S0011] With that said, I'll now turn the program over to Mr. Vandervolk. [S0012] Please go ahead, sir.

[P001] [S0013] Eric Vandervalk [109]: Good morning. [S0014] Thank you for your interest in Ollie's. [S0015] Our teams did a great job of delivering strong fourth quarter results and setting us up for accelerated growth. [S0016] Our fourth quarter comparable store sales growth of 2.8% was in line with our expectations and we delivered better than expected adjusted earnings. [S0017] We are particularly pleased with these results given the compressed holiday season and which required a back-to-back ad calendar and raised the operational complexity of the quarter. [S0018] Our team executed very well, and we were ready for the surge in demand that we saw in the days leading up to Christmas. [S0019] In fact, December was our strongest month of the quarter. [S0020] Consumers remain under pressure and are seeking value. [S0021] Many retailers are closing stores or shutting down entirely. [S0022] Tariffs are creating uncertainty across the retail landscape. [S0023] This all bodes well for Ollie's. [S0024] As a closeout retailer, we are constantly looking for the best product opportunities in the market. [S0025] The same goes for how we think about investing our capital to drive long-term shareholder value. [S0026] With so many retailers closing stores or going bankrupt in the past year, there are a considerable number of abandoned customers, merchandise, real estate, and talent in the marketplace. [S0027] We think there's an opportunity to take on some of these assets in a manner that strengthens our competitive positioning, broadens our footprint, and bolsters shareholder returns for years to come. [S0028] We recently announced an agreement to acquire 40 additional store leases of former Big Lots locations. [S0029] These stores are the right size, located in our existing trade areas, and have been serving a value-oriented shopper for many years. [S0030] In addition, they come with below-market rents and long-term leases that give us control of these properties for upwards of 20 to 30 years. [S0031] As a result, these stores are capable of generating outsized profitability over the long term. [S0032] One of the hallmarks of Ali's is our ability to generate profitable growth and consistent returns for our shareholders. [S0033] This is a very stable business model. [S0034] The closeout market is massive and there will always be merchandise available for a variety of reasons. [S0035] Innovation, packaging changes, shifts in consumer demand, store closures, tariffs, uncertainty, and other unforeseen events. [S0036] These are just some of the drivers of the closeout market. [S0037] While sources of products are constantly changing, the availability of closeouts is stable and consistent. [S0038] With our flexible buying model, we are in control of what we buy and when we buy it. [S0039] If a product does not meet our requirements, either from a pricing, quality, or branding perspective, we simply don't buy it. [S0040] Price is certainly a very important component to our value proposition, but it's not the only component. [S0041] We deliver value to our customers through a unique and ever-changing assortment of products that combine price, quality, and national brands. [S0042] Selling good stuff cheap has been our purpose since our founding over 42 years ago. [S0043] And this remains our passion and motivation to this day. [S0044] In closing, let me just say how excited about the future of Ali's. [S0045] With our strong value proposition, flexible buying model, profitable and portable store concept, fortress balance sheet, and talented, hardworking associates, we are well positioned to continue driving profitable growth. [S0046] Now on to Rob, who will discuss our fourth quarter results and guidance for the new fiscal year.

[P002] [S0047] Robert Helm [332]: Rob. [S0048] Thanks, Eric, and good morning, everyone. [S0049] We were pleased with our results and trends in the fourth quarter. [S0050] We grew comparable store sales in line with expectations and deliver adjusted earnings ahead of our expectations, despite facing some pressure from unfavorable weather and the liquidation of the big lot stores. [S0051] Before we run through the numbers, it's also important to point out that there are some transitory expenses related to bankruptcy-acquired stores and our accelerated growth. [S0052] While this puts a little pressure on our near-term earnings growth, it should also lead to stronger earnings power for 2026 and beyond. [S0053] In the quarter, net sales increased 3% to $667 million, driven by new stores and comparable sales growth, partially offset by the impact of last year's 53rd week. [S0054] As a reminder, the 53rd week generated $34 million in sales and about 4 cents to earnings per share last year. [S0055] Excluding the extra week of sales in the comparison, net sales increased 8.5%. [S0056] Copper Bowl store sales in the fourth quarter increased 2.8%, driven by fairly equal increases in both transactions and baskets. [S0057] Our best performing categories in the quarter were housewares, food and candy, electronics, and room air. [S0058] Ali's Army members increased over 8% to over 15.1 million members in the quarter, and sales to our members represented over 80% of total sales. [S0059] Consistent with prior trends, we continue to drive growth in our younger customer demographic and the retention of higher income customers. [S0060] We ended the quarter with 559 stores in 31 states, an increase of 9% year over year. [S0061] We opened 13 new stores in the quarter and 50 for the fiscal year. [S0062] Our new stores continue to perform well, including the former 99 cent only stores and the first wave of acquired Big Lots stores. [S0063] Gross margin increased 20 basis points to 40.7%, primarily from lower supply chain costs, partially offset by a slightly lower merchandise margin driven by mix. [S0064] SG&A expenses of $170 million included a one-time expense of $5.5 million for the accelerated expense resulting from the modification of existing equity awards for our executive chairman. [S0065] Excluding this one-time expense, SG&A as a percentage of net sales increased 50 basis points to 24.6%, primarily from our accelerating store growth and the earlier timing of new store openings in fiscal 2025. [S0066] Pre-opening expenses were $5 million in the quarter. [S0067] Most of the increase was from the earlier timing of new store openings compared to fiscal 2024. [S0068] We have already opened 16 stores in fiscal 2025. [S0069] This time last year, we had not even opened a single store yet. [S0070] Dark rent associated with the bankruptcy-acquired stores also contributed to the increase in pre-opening expenses and was $1 million in the quarter. [S0071] Moving down to the bottom line, adjusted net income and adjusted earnings per share were $73 million and $1.19 respectively. [S0072] Lastly, adjusted EBITDA was $109 million and adjusted EBITDA margin was 16.4% for the quarter. [S0073] Turning to the balance sheet, our financial position remains very strong. [S0074] Cash and short-term investments were $429 million at the end of the quarter, and we had no outstanding borrowings under a revolving credit facility. [S0075] Our strong balance sheet is a strategic asset for us. [S0076] In 2024, we were able to deliver against our expectations while setting our path to accelerated growth in 2025. [S0077] We opportunistically acquired a number of stores out of bankruptcy, began building the inventory to fill these stores, and made the necessary investments in our supply chain. [S0078] all while remaining committed to our share repurchase program. [S0079] Inventories increased 9% year over year, primarily driven by our accelerating store growth and the earlier kins of new store openings in 2025. [S0080] On a per store basis, inventories were relatively flat year over year. [S0081] Capital expenditures totaled $24 million for the quarter, with the majority of the spending going towards the opening of new stores, the maintenance of existing stores, and enhancements to our distribution centers. [S0082] The Big Lots locations were generally well maintained and have required limited build-out expenses to open thus far. [S0083] Along with earnings today, we also announced a new $300 million share buyback program in a separate press release. [S0084] While accelerated growth is our primary focus in the short term, we remain committed to returning capital to our investors through share repurchases while balancing our strategic growth opportunities and working capital needs. [S0085] Lastly, Let me provide some commentary on our initial outlook and how we are thinking about the upcoming fiscal year. [S0086] As most of you know, our long-term annual growth algorithm is 10% unit growth, comparable store sales growth of 1% to 2%, gross margin of 40%, slight SG&A expense leverage as a percentage of sales, some modest benefit from share repurchases and investment income, resulting in low double-digit adjusted earnings growth. [S0087] With the acquisition of the former big lot stores, we are uniquely positioned to accelerate our growth and gain market share. [S0088] As Eric discussed, we have been building up to this moment and are well positioned to take advantage of this unique opportunity. [S0089] Our current plan is to open approximately 75 new stores this year. [S0090] New store openings will be more heavily weighted to the first half, with approximately 21 stores in the first quarter and 65% in the first half. [S0091] The big lots locations will incur a higher pre-opening expenses because we take possession of these earlier than a typical opening. [S0092] The dark rent is expected to be around $5 million for the year or six cents to adjusted earnings per share. [S0093] We have included all of this in our initial guidance and we'll also quantify the dark rent expenses related to the acquired big lots locations as we report the quarters. [S0094] Not included in our guidance is any benefit to comparable store sales from the big lots stores closures. [S0095] We remain confident that this will be a net benefit to us in fiscal 2025, but it's difficult to predict how and when this will play out. [S0096] The majority of the Big Lot stores are still in the process of closing or have very recently just closed, and our sample size is still relatively small. [S0097] In the handful of overlapping markets where the Big Lot stores have been closed for longer than a few weeks, our stores in these markets are coming better than our stores outside of those markets. [S0098] With all of that said, our initial guidance for fiscal 2025 is the following. [S0099] Approximately 75 new store openings, total net sales of $2.564 to $2.586 billion, comparable store sales growth of 1% to 2%, gross margin of approximately 40%, operating income of $283 to $292 million, adjusted net income of $225 to $232 million, and adjusted net income per diluted share of $3 to $65 to $3.75. [S0100] These estimates assume depreciation and amortization expenses of $54 million, inclusive of $14 million within cost of goods sold, reopening expenses of $21 million, which includes dark rent of approximately $5 million related to the acquired Big Lots locations, an annual effective tax rate of 25 percent, which excludes the tax benefits related to stock-based compensation, diluted weighted average shares outstanding of approximately $62 million, and capital expenditures of approximately $83 to $88 million, which includes the build-out of the Big Lot stores. [S0101] Lastly, let me give you some thoughts on how we're thinking about the quarterly comp cadence. [S0102] The first quarter got off to a sluggish start. [S0103] However, we have seen momentum start to build with a change in the weather. [S0104] As we get further into the year, we face tougher comparisons in June and July from lapping the strong air conditioner sales last year. [S0105] Then in the back half, the comparisons start to ease a bit, from lapping the Big Lots door closures. [S0106] As a result, we're thinking that comp growth could be in the lower end of the 1% to 2% range for the first half, and the midpoint to the higher end of the range for the 1% to 2% in the back half. [S0107] Now back to Eric.

[P003] [S0108] Eric Vandervalk [846]: Thanks, Rob. [S0109] This is a very exciting time for us at Ollie's. [S0110] The foundation of our success is our people. [S0111] I am very appreciative and proud of what we have accomplished as a result of their hard work and commitment. [S0112] Our people care deeply and find purpose in serving customers and stretching their hard-earned dollars. [S0113] This is especially important in this moment. [S0114] We are. [S0115] This concludes our prepared remarks. [S0116] We are now happy to answer your questions.

[P004] [S0117] Operator [882]: Certainly. [S0118] And our first question for today comes from the line of Steven Zaccone from Citi. [S0119] Your question, please.

[P005] [S0120] Steven Zaccone [889]: All right, good morning. [S0121] Thanks very much for taking my question. [S0122] I was curious for your assessment on the consumer. [S0123] You kind of gave some commentary there about how trends have performed quarter to date. [S0124] But if you take a step back, how do you think about the state of your consumer? [S0125] How's that factored into your outlook for 2025? [S0126] Thanks, Steve.
[S0127] Eric Vandervalk [909]: Appreciate the question. [S0128] Consumers remain under pressure. [S0129] We thrive in this environment. [S0130] Ollie's is the destination for any type of disruption, whether it's consumers under pressure, excess inventory resulting from store closures, tariff pressure, people to join our team, real estate. [S0131] But back to the consumer, our consumable business continues to be a very strong business for us and a traffic driver, which is certainly indicative of where the mindset of the consumer is. [S0132] The consumer continues to respond to amazing deals, whether they're John Potter, The discretionary categories or non discretionary categories and it ollie's value always wins this being said, big ticket items have been a little softer. [S0133] John Potter, In terms of household income segments, the trade down continues higher income consumers, we define as over 100,000 household income we continue to see that trade down. [S0134] John Potter, And retention of those customers we're seeing continuously strong low middle income. [S0135] cohort at the $40,000 to $65,000 range, and our low-income cohort has been stable.

[P006] [S0136] Steven Zaccone [983]: Okay, thanks for that. [S0137] My follow-up is on gross margin. [S0138] So, 2024 came in better than your 40% algo. [S0139] You know, the guide is for 40% this year. [S0140] Can you just help us think through the puts and takes? [S0141] Like, can supply chain costs still be a good guy as we think about 2025? [S0142] Sure, Steve.
[S0143] Robert Helm [1000]: From a gross margin perspective, I would say that Our algo is 40%. [S0144] Anytime that we see ourselves exceeding 40%, we reinvest in the customer and pricing to drive loyalty. [S0145] From a supply chain perspective, we're planning for a mostly stable environment. [S0146] So supply chain costs will be flattish year over year, aside from the benefit we get from burning in the Princeton DC that we opened last year. [S0147] We have planned for shrink similar to how we planned for shrink in 2024, although we're starting to see the shrink headwinds soften a little bit over the last, say, 200 stores or so that we've counted. [S0148] From a buying, you know, getting back to IMU and a buying perspective, we expect that the buying environment could be quite good coming into the mid-year and the back half. [S0149] as some of this slowdown in consumer demand and sales for some other full-price retailers starts to play out and the tariff impact starts to play out. [S0150] So overall, we're very comfortable with our 40% gross margin, considered some small tariff impact in there in the short term, and we think we're ready to deliver for 2025. [S0151] Great.

[P007] [S0152] Chuck Grom [1099]: Hey. [S0153] Good morning, Eric. [S0154] Good morning, Rob. [S0155] On the biggie front, was the headwind to sales commensurate with your plan of about 50 basis points in the fourth quarter? [S0156] And more recently, now that the liquidations have passed at most of the locations, have you seen an inflection in sales? [S0157] And then just bigger picture, zooming out, what have been the biggest learnings thus far on the big lots front from a from an operational and talent front?
[S0158] Robert Helm [1125]: Sure, I'll take the first part. [S0159] I think Eric will take the second part. [S0160] The Big Lots impact was not quite what we expected. [S0161] When we guided the quarter in the early part of December, we did not anticipate or foresee the deal with Nexus falling through. [S0162] So the complete closure of the chain and liquidation in January and February was not something that we planned for or guided to. [S0163] And just to kind of level set everyone on what actually occurred in the quarter, we started to see some small benefit in comps in surrounding stores from the store closures that closed in October and November. [S0164] That was about 100 stores. [S0165] And then we had about 100 stores that liquidated in the fourth quarter where we didn't see as much of a headwind as we anticipated. [S0166] because it appears that those stores were relatively starved of fresh inventory for holiday, and that inventory was diverted to the go-forward chain. [S0167] When they made the announcement at the end of December and then the ensuing liquidation in January and February, we saw quite a bit of headwind relative to that. [S0168] However, January and February also overlapped some really unseasonably cold weather and winter storms, so it's very hard to parse out what the exact impact to the liquidation was in January and February. [S0169] Now that we've cleared the liquidation and the weather is changing, we have seen quite a step change in our momentum and our comps and still hard to parse out. [S0170] So we did not embed in our guidance. [S0171] As you folks know, we are relatively conservative folks. [S0172] We like to continue to deliver for our shareholders and our investors. [S0173] So we thought it prudent to give the 1% to 2% guidance But if you take a step back on the total market share opportunity for Big Lots, it's a very unique situation where Big Lots didn't really close too many stores as they struggled over the last couple of years. [S0174] And their last reported annual revenue base was in the range of $4.5 billion. [S0175] So when you take into account they did about 25% of their business in furniture, and you subtract that out, and then you subtract out the markets that we're not in, which there's about an 80% to 85% overlap on the original Big Lots fleet in our store base, you get to a number that's a $2.7 billion addressable market share opportunity. [S0176] And we like our chances to grab that market share as much as anyone.
[S0177] Eric Vandervalk [1291]: Yeah, Chuck, the second part of your question related to operational line up with Big Lots employees. [S0178] We've had a lot of success in recruiting leaders, especially in the field, store leaders and at district level. [S0179] Operationally, the companies were similar enough that Big Lots people, when they come into the OLLI's environment, hit the ground running. [S0180] They certainly have some very great people And we're very happy that we've been able to recruit them and have them join our team. [S0181] It helps us to run fast, especially in some of these new stores that we're picking up, the former Big Lot stores. [S0182] We're picking up leaders and associates in those stores. [S0183] It helps us to get a faster, more meaningful start as we grand open those stores. [S0184] We're also finding that the conversion of Big Lot stores to an Ali store is even a little easier than we expected. [S0185] It's going faster and potentially is, you know, fairly economical. [S0186] So all things are lining up very nicely for all those big lot stores that are now in our pipeline to convert to Ali's in 2025.

[P008] [S0187] Chuck Grom [1375]: Great answer. [S0188] That's great to hear. [S0189] Just a quick follow-up. [S0190] Can you discuss the progress you've made with the role of the private label credit card? [S0191] Maybe how many states or stores now offer the card and are

[P009] [S0192] Matthew Boss [1395]: You guys still there? [S0193] Jonathan?
[S0194] Eric Vandervalk [1396]: Hello? [S0195] Yes, here.
[S0196] Eric Vandervalk [1398]: Yeah, I think Chuck cut out, but I think we understand the question around the credit card. [S0197] Is everyone else still on, I guess? [S0198] Yes, everyone is still on. [S0199] I'll go ahead and answer. [S0200] All right, excellent. [S0201] We just lost Chuck. [S0202] So yeah, on the credit card, we've rolled it out to most stores. [S0203] By the end of Q1, we will have rolled it out to the chain. [S0204] It's too early to report in on what it's going to ultimately mean to our business. [S0205] We love it as an enhancement to our Ollie's Army loyalty program. [S0206] And we're seeing initially the basket size for an Ollie's credit card customer is fairly significantly higher than the basket size for an Ollie's Army customer who does not have a credit card. [S0207] So it looks very promising. [S0208] By the end of the Q1, we'll be rolled out to the whole chain and we'll see what it means for the balance of the year.

[P010] [S0209] Alexia Morgan [1461]: Hi, this is Alexia Morgan on for Peter Keith at Piper Sandler. [S0210] Thanks for taking our question. [S0211] I was wondering if you could speak more to the dead rent dynamic on a going forward basis. [S0212] You quantified dark rent as $5 million in 2025, so it seems like it could impact flow through this year. [S0213] So we were wondering then how to think about flow through dynamics in the model from 2025 to 2026, how it could change.
[S0214] Robert Helm [1493]: Sure, I'll take that, Mr. Rob. [S0215] We're very excited about what accelerated growth means for 2025 and what it means for 2026 and beyond. [S0216] The big lot store closures have given us a unique opportunity to really improve our strategic positioning, broaden our footprint, and boost our returns. [S0217] The bankruptcy-acquired rent stores require that we're on the clock for rent as soon as the store is turned over to us. [S0218] In that model, we have to take on, on average, about four months of dead rent versus a typical Ollie's opening, which is four to five weeks. [S0219] these stores come with below market rents and long-term leases which allow for outsized profitability for this segment of stores given that these stores are going to open midway through the year into the back half of the year you don't get as much flow through on the on the earnings for the for the store for the year and it is burdened with the dead rent uh which makes it about 300 000 or so a store if it was a normal year uh you know we we would deliver say, you know, low-teens earnings growth, and when I'm talking about 2026, we'd expect 2026 to be to mid-teens earnings growth, maybe even approaching high-teens earnings growth. [S0220] And that's casting aside any market share grab or outsized comp that we would deliver in 25 or 26 by virtue of acquiring the big lots market share aside from the real estate.

[P011] [S0221] Alexia Morgan [1584]: Okay, thank you. [S0222] And then maybe just one more. [S0223] You had already talked a little bit about the Big Lots opportunity, but one more about that. [S0224] How are you thinking about the new Big Lots stores opening as compared to the new 99-cent-only stores which you had acquired, which seemed to be very strong and successful right out of the gate? [S0225] So we were just wondering how the Big Lots stores could have a similar experience.
[S0226] Eric Vandervalk [1615]: Sure, Alexia. [S0227] We think about them very similarly. [S0228] In fact, we are more bullish on a big lots conversion than we were even on a 99 conversion. [S0229] And as you know, we were very bullish on 99 cent only conversion. [S0230] The biggest, you know, attributes these two companies provide to us is these are, I call them warm boxes. [S0231] A lot of the real estate we do traditionally over many years, is second-generation sites that have been vacant for years. [S0232] They've been vacant so long you forget who the retailer was that was in the box. [S0233] So cold sites, these are all warm. [S0234] Not only are they warm, they're also warm with customers who have been conditioned, discount customers conditioned to shop in a store concept that's similar enough to us. [S0235] and a customer cohort that's similar enough to our customers. [S0236] So we have just a little bit of experience to date with Big Lots conversions. [S0237] Only a handful have been converted so far, but we really like what we're seeing on the conversions in terms of the excitement of the customer. [S0238] And so the initial sales reads, we think it'll be as strong or even stronger than 99 cent only conversions.

[P012] [S0239] Matthew Boss [1709]: Great. [S0240] Thanks. [S0241] So, Eric, maybe could you elaborate on the cadence of first quarter to date same store sales? [S0242] What you saw early versus the exit rate in February and more recent trends you've seen in March? [S0243] And have you embedded any lift in the full year guide for potential market share opportunity tied to Big Lots?
[S0244] Eric Vandervalk [1731]: Sure. [S0245] Great question, Matt. [S0246] I'm going to ask Rob to address.
[S0247] Robert Helm [1736]: Hey, Matt. [S0248] How are you? [S0249] February was a pretty tough month. [S0250] There were quite a bit of headwinds. [S0251] There was weather. [S0252] There was the Big Lots door closures. [S0253] There was a delay early on in tax refunds, although that's caught up and now started to accelerate. [S0254] And there's been widespread media reports of slowdown in consumer demand. [S0255] So it was quite volatile. [S0256] With that being said, we've seen a very recent step change towards the end of February into the early part of March, which coincides with the big lot store closures and the change in the weather. [S0257] And we have some pretty good momentum at this moment. [S0258] As of now, we are running quarter to date in line with our comp guidance for the first quarter. [S0259] But we have a lot of spring selling to go. [S0260] The weather hasn't quite fully changed yet. [S0261] And we're pretty confident that we're going to be able to deliver. [S0262] And as you know, you follow the story a long time. [S0263] We don't turn the registers off.

[P013] [S0264] Matthew Boss [1799]: Got it. [S0265] And then maybe just a follow-up. [S0266] Eric, Could you argue Ollie's could actually be a net beneficiary of tariffs as we tie in availability and product that you're seeing? [S0267] And Rob, on the SG&A front, if we exclude the dead rent, how best to think about the comp needed to leverage SG&A in 2025? [S0268] And then multi-year, what's the right comp leverage point you think for the model?
[S0269] Eric Vandervalk [1825]: So yeah, Matt, on tariffs, it's It's kind of back to how I answered the state of consumer question. [S0270] Tariffs are disruptive. [S0271] They're especially disruptive when they change moment to moment. [S0272] We thrive on disruption. [S0273] So this is a great example of disruption. [S0274] I think when you look at it in the short term, we're a price follower. [S0275] We focus on maintaining price gaps to our competitive set, delivering strong values. [S0276] We don't have a mandate to buy anything. [S0277] So if it's priced right, It meets our margin profile. [S0278] We buy it. [S0279] If it's not priced right, we don't buy it. [S0280] It's a very flexible model. [S0281] So we have a business model that is really built for a situation like this, where there are various products that are incurring certain expenses. [S0282] We can choose not to buy them, or we could follow the market in terms of price. [S0283] So in terms of product availability, absolutely. [S0284] When you look back on the history and our experience with tariffs, from some years going back, it does result in excess inventory that's available to buy back. [S0285] We would expect that to happen most likely in the back half of 2025 if it follows the same pattern that it did back when tariffs were increased five-ish years ago.
[S0286] Robert Helm [1906]: From an SG&A perspective, for 2025, we'd expect SG&A leverage to be pretty much at the midpoint of the 1% to 2% positive comp. [S0287] We operate off a relatively low G&A base, and we have the corporate investments in place to be able to support our accelerated growth. [S0288] There may be some wiggling from quarter to quarter from a SG&A expense leverage flow-through perspective as we're accelerating growth and we're putting in some of those upper field investments to be able to build out new markets. [S0289] But on the year, we'd expect it to be closer than midpoint.

[P014] [S0290] Brad Thomas [1959]: Hi. [S0291] Thanks, and good morning. [S0292] Maybe just to follow up on Matt's question on tariffs. [S0293] Can you talk a little bit more about how those are baked into your guidance overall and the exposure that you have on the direct import side?
[S0294] Eric Vandervalk [1973]: Sure. [S0295] Exposure on the direct import side, again, very, very short term.
